512.prompt: I opened the window and heard a distant bell. Beneath it, I could also hear
512.completion:
sounds coming from the city – the sound of cars and the metro. It was the 25th of January, a national holiday in Israel. Hiding from relatives (and being one of the few who could enjoy the holiday), I decided to see things from the birds’ perspective.

The square tree was planted in 2012. Although trees are often planted to mark special events, I wouldn’t know which one led to the planting of this particular tree – it wasn’t even clear to me whether the tree had additional symbolic significance. At first I thought that the markings and trimming were done in a very complex manner, but with a slight magnification I discovered something fascinating: Only seven out of the nine branches resemble a square. Clearly, the tree was trimmed manually by the gardener, whose steady hand enabled them to recreate the square-like form. It took a significant amount of work and attention, which must be repeated once a year.

Watching the tree again and again I also noticed that despite the perfect trimming, the pace of the tree’s growth is slightly different from the one in the square. The gardener must have realised this and every once in a while added an additional piece of plywood to the already existing square. The plywood was attached with small strings that were tied to small nails. Only when looking at the tree from afar could one discover these small nails, which are a reflection of both the gardener’s devotion and the labour that exists in order to preserve the tree and keep its image intact.

As the tree grows, it seems that the gardener prefers to constantly raise the plywood and attach another plywood in its place rather than adjust the existing plywood. While photographing, I couldn’t stop thinking about this tree. I became certain that this same story was reflected in everything around, in the world of people, in work, and in the processes of life. We mostly prefer to act in an easy and familiar way, adding and changing rather than changing ourselves. It will be interesting to see the tree in the following years – whether I’ll discover additional squares between these ever-growing, always changing, and not very well-mannered branches.<eos>
